The idea behind "The Great Gatsby" was to take a famous novel, strip out everything that doesn't belong, and rework it into the most perfect movie about the rich, powerful young man that ever lived -- "Gatsby in motion," according to the film's director, Baz Luhrmann. Here's what he told the New Yorker in the 1990s.

On the origin of "Poverty"

He didn't quite get it yet. [Director] Tony Richardson was a friend I was working with at the time on The Phantom of the Opera and The Phantom of the Opera II. He and I had both heard about a novel called Poverty by [Frank] Lentricchia [the father of film criticism], who was a great admirer of Ernest Hemingway and [his book] The Sun Also Rises. Our mutual friends thought we'd make a good team. We had the story and the structure. He had the talent. I had the passion. We both agreed it all needed to be done right.

On the origins of "The Great Gatsby"

Lentricchia was a bit of the genius behind the film and also the name of the main character. The great thing about Lentricchia was that he wrote the book when he was 40 years old, and that's how I was introduced. I was 27, had two kids at home and was divorced. His book is about a young Gatsby. The name Gatsby has been in use since the 18th century, but it doesn't come up very often these days. But they loved the name, and Lentricchia said, "Let's use it for the character." I told Tony, "It's a cool name, but do it as it's been used for 200 years, and it'll be good." It's the same with Gatsby.

On "The Glass Menagerie"

I got the job on it by accident. I was shooting some scenes with Tony Richardson in Italy and someone told me they were looking for someone to come in who could shoot some stuff, and I told them, "I can do that! It's only like six months.' And that was that, except that the job turned into four or five years, and I wanted to do it so bad. To be able to do these films like "Poverty" and the other films I made, I couldn't do them all at once. So I went and had to do a lot of work from different directors -- Peter Bogdanovich and Mike Nichols were two -- and at one point I'd been doing it for four or five years. I was so exhausted!

On the relationship between "Gatsby" and The Great Gatsby

My theory at first was that the thing about the old book that appealed about the young Gatsby was that it felt the way he was being portrayed. It was a character who was in his 30s but didn't feel in his 30s. It was all about youngness. I think that was why I thought, "I'm doing a story about a man who starts young but never stops." But then it turned out we have the same idea.

Fifty-eight years ago today, a group of students and their coach were involved in an accident just north of the U.S.-Canadian border. It resulted in a horrific death as well as the beginnings of what would later become a much larger story.

In June of 1965, the Toronto St. Clair & Huron Railway—now part of the Canadian National Railroad—was carrying seven students and their coach to a volleyball match in Canada. The passengers were planning to disembark at Niagara Falls to attend a night party; however, the coach was driving, and it soon became clear that the train was about to get out of control when it approached the bridge over the Horseshoe Falls. The train stalled on the bridge. At around 2:00 p.m., it suddenly derailed.

The first car that flipped out of control crashed into a nearby bridge, killing all seven passengers to a total of 21 in all. Those killed ranged in age from 16 to 42. Only one girl was aged 14.

Frozen 2, the sequel to the 2013 Disney hit "Frozen," is opening in limited release this weekend, but a new report says that the budget is so large, there may never be a sequel. The report came from the New York Times.

According to sources familiar with the budget, the movie is currently worth as much as $700 million — and that's just for the songs: the budget also includes production and marketing, costumes, and locations. There's also the cost of creating new characters. Frozen 2 is on track to be so expensive that Disney will need to sell at least 3.5 million tickets at the domestic box office to break even.

But Disney doesn't really need to break even — it just needs to find the revenue. The original Frozen's global grosses topped $1.07 billion worldwide — including $1.02 billion domestically — in its first two weeks. So the studio has a lot riding on the success of Frozen 2 on its upcoming release in November and beyond.

"People don't know what to expect when you open a movie like "Frozen." The first one was so well loved, the studio saw this as an opportunity to give people another one. So what would have been a franchise, in my view, would be an opportunity to do something new with that, and build on that excitement," said Phil Contrino, CEO of BoxOffice.com.

So when Frozen 2 gets released, and it will happen sooner rather than later, the studio isn't just looking for a solid take. For starters, they need to create excitement among young girls and boys who have grown up with the first film. "I think it's important to note that Disney has never gone out of their way to make more sequels. That's just something that they do that Disney does," said Contrino.

According to Disney Chief Creative Officer Chris Buck, they want to create a sequel that "isn't just another sequel," and that means spending $650 to $750 million or so.

Frozen was originally made as an animated feature, but went on to be a hit and earned $1.3 billion at the box office. But it also helped Disney's live-action offerings make money. The studio is releasing a live-action Snow White and the Huntsman, which is scheduled for release Oct. 13. The studio is also bringing back Beauty and the Beast, the story of a man and a beautiful woman who fall in love and become lovers, in spring 2016.

There are still some questions about the film, particularly with a live-action Princess Anna. According to the latest reports, Anna will reportedly be a young woman. But the last time a female Disney princess had a serious relationship with another woman, her love interest died after the romance. "There will be lots of speculation around what's going to happen with Anna. It's up to them to give a complete and honest response," said New York Times critic Alyssa Rosenberg.

While Disney might need more money upfront, it's important to acknowledge that every budget is not the same. The studio made more money on "Frozen" than any movie made so far this year, and that will be one factor the studio will use.

"These were very expensive movies on the marketing end. And what we're seeing here is exactly how these movies play; a huge amount of marketing and a very expensive movie," said Contrino.

If Frozen 2 performs big with fans and box office, there are big payoffs for Disney.

"Disney is going to get a lot of people who had never heard of Disney movies," said Contrino. "For a little over half of this movie's audience, "Frozen" is going to be part of their 'family' experience forever."

Redskins quarterback Kirk Cousins told reporters on Monday that the team has received a "pretty good" deal to let him hit the open market.

"I'm going to start in camp and take a good look around," Cousins said. "If I feel that I like where I'm going and the opportunity is there, I plan on playing."

While there were rumblings in recent weeks that the Redskins might try to trade Cousins, his comments give us some idea of what he might ask for.

On one hand, the Redskins could easily go into camp and sign Cousins for $20 million per season, but they'd still have to give him an extension. That might be a tough sell with head coach Jay Gruden and the team in rebuilding mode.

On the other hand, it's probably not too early for the coach to look at whether a franchise quarterback still fits with his overall philosophy, something that could change in a hurry.

Cousins said the team doesn't view him as someone who needs to be held back.

"I don't have anything that says for me what the situation is going to be around camp," Cousins said. "I'm going to make the best decision for me and the organization at the time."

For those unfamiliar with the name, it's a place called the Hualapai Nation Reservation. It's an old, sprawling place where the only paved road winds all around the perimeter of it.

The reservation is an offshoot of a much larger reservation that's been in place since 1848. The Hualapai are a Native American tribe from the Southwest. They had their own land and settlement before the Spanish arrived. They also have their own language.

It's important to note that it has been nearly 2,000 years since the first Spanish settlers began coming to the area. A lot has changed in about that time period too, including some of the people and cultural ideas that have developed over that time.

The Hualapai were granted a portion of their land back in 1848 for just over 1,000 acres, which was smaller than they needed. But for some reason, the government decided that they didn't like the land and wanted to expropriate it. By the time they finally realized the error of their ways, the Spanish had left.

Some of those who stayed in the region continued to fight the government, especially in the 1840s. And when the Hualapai found out in the late 1800s that Spanish settlers were using their land as a grazing ground, it wasn't about being on their land. They took action in response.

In 1905, the government tried to expropriate the entire reservation to build a road to the Pacific. They tried to convince the United States, Great Britain and Mexico to buy it and give it to them, but none of those talks went anywhere.

There wasn't anyone else in the world with more land than the Hualapai, except the United States. A lot of that land was taken by the U.S. government or by the Spanish. When the land was returned to the Hualapai, the land was divided up into lots, which they then used for grazing. Most of the reservation isn't actually used for grazing, except during the fall and winter months when it's necessary. But when it's not possible to graze or when there are drought conditions, the reservation becomes very important to the Hualapai. It's not only about providing livestock for them and other people who live there, but they also use the reservation for recreation. It's something like a national park. That's exactly how this tribe viewed their own territory.

But in 1971, a new road was constructed for the construction of a highway. This road was meant for vehicles, not people and the Hualapai didn't like that. They petitioned the court that was ruling on the matter and argued that the road was the sole reason the reservation was divided up in this way. The court sided with the Hialapai and ruled against the National Park Service. They essentially wanted to deny the Hualapai this important and beautiful place for recreation. The road construction was halted and the reservation reverted back to what it originally was: a reservation for livestock.

That's how the Hualapai had fought to prevent the construction of the highway. In 1976, the road was eventually approved and paved. But it was at that point that there was a second petition to the court. They wanted the highway to be stopped at that point. They tried to convince the court that the Hialapai were "in danger," that their land would be lost and the land could be used for farming.

That was in 1979 when the ruling came in. It was a unanimous decision. The court said that the land they had been using in that way was not "unused" and could be used for grazing as it was. As for the argument that they were "in danger," the court said that the Hialapai were using their land as a place of cultural, spiritual and spiritual significance and "the cultural value of Indian Country outweighed the 'potential harm' that would come from such action."

That was a big blow in the history of the reservation. The idea of an Indian land, unoccupied, was no longer an option. It would be used for grazing. That's basically what happened.

The Hialapai have faced a pretty difficult and difficult time ever since. To make matters worse, many people who have traveled to the Hualapai reservation aren't able to enjoy the place. The number of Americans who suffer from a chronic mental illness has reached alarming levels, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced Thursday. The CDC also found that an estimated 725,000 Americans have an ongoing mental illness.

The new numbers represent the highest prevalence of mental illness ever reported at the state or federal levels, a trend that echoes the explosion of mental illness observed when the World War II and Korean War saw the onset of tens of millions of patients struggling with depression, anxiety and other physical symptoms. That era's mental health crisis also brought about an epidemic of schizophrenia, as many soldiers returning from combat returned from mental illness.

The CDC reported that the prevalence of those diagnosed with serious mental illness doubled in the past decade, with 1 in 12 Americans suffering from serious mental illness. The new statistics are also particularly alarming considering that the United States has one of the highest unemployment rates for the mentally ill in the world and that only a small fraction of those diagnosed with serious mental illness are receiving any sort of treatment.

The CDC's study, "Persistent Mental Illness, Homelessness, and Substance Use Among the Homeless," showed that the incidence of homelessness rose sharply between 2002 and 2007, with one homeless person becoming homeless every 42 seconds for the first time since the agency began tracking homelessness in 1991.

The study also showed that nearly 45 percent of homeless men aged 20 to 49 had one or more serious mental illnesses that required hospital treatment.

"This increase is concerning," said CDC Director Dr. Tom Frieden. "It means people aren't receiving proper care and can't stay safely in their homes, and as more people struggle with serious mental health problems, there's an increased risk that these events would turn deadly."

There is evidence that the United States is at risk for a larger mental health crisis than many other countries around the world. According to the International Foundation for Suicide Prevention, more than 2.2 million Americans attempt suicide each year; another 2.1 million attempt suicide in the year after they attempted it.

This is a continuation of the previous episode where I took a look at the "new" Android Security Patterns. This time I'll look at the other new ones (but have them from Android Studio). Here is another one: Insecure Read-Only Memory.

Insecure Read-Only Memory

At some point, Android has to handle write and read access to memory. It does so with various libraries like Android's RKS library, System UI, as well as various drivers for the ARM-based SoC. For a number of reasons, it's difficult to have this managed correctly when developing applications – particularly those that are using these drivers to run. There is a potential problem though, if the application is run in a location that does allow write and read access from the user. That would allow for malicious code to be run. This is a problem that has been around for a while. It's basically common sense that you shouldn't run your code in a vulnerable location that can be accessed at any given time by anyone.

So how can we manage this appropriately if we are building the application, and not running the app and being able to execute it? Android has been around a long time, so there have been multiple attempts to solve this problem. These are what I consider to be the "new" strategies for dealing with this. As you can see from the diagram, the problem is that the memory is allocated in a read-only fashion. Because of this, the programmer is not able to see all of the contents of this memory until it has been written out to user-written memory. A write could happen at any time. As a result, it is not possible for an app to determine the current ownership of the memory – or to determine the "owner" of any given object. This limits the app to only certain objects.

If the app is on the same process as the system process, it will be able to detect if the app is running or being manipulated. It can also check for a process ownership change, but if it fails that test, it can only determine the current process ownership. The issue with this approach is that if the app is running in a location that is accessible to the system without write protection, an attacker will be able to read or write data on this memory. That is why apps should not be used in this situation, and a process ownership change should be required to protect the system.

Fortunately, the security of Java applications is pretty strong. As such, we should not have to worry about this issue with Java applications. This is still a potential security concern on Android, so hopefully Android will implement a better solution.

As I mentioned earlier, the Android developers decided to include a version of RKS with the API, which will allow more direct access to the memory. It is still not guaranteed, though, that this is good enough. So let's take a look at those older Android security patterns.

Insecure Direct Memory Access

We saw the Insecure Read-Only Memory approach taken earlier. The idea is that we have an app that has access to the system memory. The "owner" of this memory is unknown. But there is still a security issue here. If a malicious app wants to try to write to memory outside of the app, it could potentially corrupt the data. That is, it would allow malicious code to be run. This also limits our application to only certain structures.

The solution here is to do an alloc/free to allow the app to get a handle to the memory. This is all the functionality of the Insecure Read-Only Memory approach taken to its logical extreme. We have no access to any memory beyond what the OS provides us with. This limits our application to only objects that are owned by the same process that's running the app. This requires an additional step that is added by the developer.

It is not a good idea to directly call these allocations to read and write the memory. This is the approach taken with this one. We can write into the memory using a native library, and then we can call the alloc function to allocate a handle to it.

In 2014, the popular video game Monster Hunter burst out of Japan and became, by far, the most successful of all Japanese video game franchises. Over four million copies of Monster Hunter were sold in Japan by the end of 2012. It is the second best selling video game franchise in Japan, behind Super Mario Kart, which has sold more than 7.2 million copies.

The popularity of Monster Hunter is thanks in part to its popularity here in the US. In the past, the series has enjoyed popularity overseas, especially with western audiences; for example, its popular anime series, Monster Hunter Zero, has been dubbed the "most watched in Japan" by Japanese TV networks.

For years, Japanese fans on YouTube—known as マモントン決定 (meppo toro) and often abbreviated to MMORPG videos—have been uploading videos covering all the ins and outs of the game. These videos have amassed over 150 million views, with many of them garnering millions of views. As a result, MMORPGs have become extremely popular in Japan, as they're highly regarded by Japanese gamers as a good place to start for budding video game players.

A large portion of the sales for Monster Hunter have been attributed to Bandai Namco itself. But is the Monster Hunter franchise really popular because it's based on a property popular in Japan?

Many video game fans argue that there are two major reasons for the popularity of Monster Hunter—the first being that all monsters in the game can be found in Japan. The game's popularity and popularity of the anime series and manga based on the game has resulted in a vast number of people from Japan and beyond being able to play and buy the game in Japan.

Many of the Japanese video game fans we spoke with in Tokyo and Osaka are adamant in believing that the video game is popular in Japan because of its Japanese popularity. The second reason for the popularity of Monster Hunter is because video games and RPGs are highly sought after in Japan for both their fun factor and for their Japanese cultural influence and accessibility.

The government shutdown is in its sixth day, and this time it doesn't seem to be stopping any progress. That's because the government's ability to meet its obligations is tied very directly to the debt ceiling.

The government is not allowed to spend more money than it pays in. This puts our national budget on a very tight leash. And thanks to a Congressional rule, spending needs to be at least three percent of gross domestic product. It was 3 percent in fiscal 2012. But last year, it was only 2.6 percent.

As I point out in my article about why Obama won the election, this 3 percent cap is crucial to our country's fiscal health. Without it, the government could not meet its obligations. Otherwise, it would start printing money. (You can read the article here.)

The reason the government is allowed to spend up to 3 percent of GDP is because Congress has agreed that it is the "national interest" to have the government run efficiently — not to simply get money from us to spend on things that make our lives more comfortable.

So as long as we agree that the government is in the country's best interest, the government will have to live within its means.

But according to the Wall Street Journal, Congress has not agreed to meet the 3 percent cap for a very long time.

This year, according to a U.S. Treasury Department spreadsheet, spending will exceed revenue for the first time since 2010. But even after the government runs out of money, its spending will outpace revenue again next year.

And Congress isn't going to agree to increase taxes on the wealthy any time soon, as the Journal notes:

Treasury also said a new revenue target of $1 trillion isn't likely anytime soon, despite President Barack Obama's $4.7 trillion plan to close the deficit in 10 years. Republicans said that a target of $800 billion would be more realistic.

The fiscal cliff has also thrown a lot of uncertainty into the government's budget plan. It could take years to come up with a solution to this problem if Congress doesn't agree to raise the debt ceiling.

And the debt ceiling could also be delayed indefinitely for this reason: as the Washington Post points out, Congress has been using the debt ceiling as a threat to increase taxes on the wealthy.

All of this has led many Republicans to call for the debt limit to be raised to avoid the government hitting its debt ceiling and then having to pay out some of the money borrowed.

But such a move would almost certainly force our already-struggling economy to break down. If the debt limit was hiked earlier, Obama might have passed a budget by now.

But of course, these Republican concerns aren't shared by most Americans.

According to the latest data (released by Gallup as of today), most Americans would like to see the nation hit the debt ceiling without any further delays.

In an online poll, conducted among more than 2,000 adults, 59 percent said they would rather have the debt ceiling not raised until 2015 at the earliest, versus just 20 percent who agreed to a debt ceiling hike earlier.

Only a minority, 38 percent, said they would like to see a higher debt ceiling than the one just imposed on the nation.

Most Americans, 69 percent, said they wouldn't like to see their personal savings and pension investments lose money in the event of a major financial crisis. Only 12 percent said they would.

And when asked how they would react if the United States faced a "catastrophic economic event," 60 percent said they would either support a government rescue plan or oppose the country defaulting on its debt. Only 15 percent said they would support default.

So why are Americans so willing to let the debt ceiling be hiked until 2015? Most likely, it's because America is in no financial danger. Americans' living standards are higher today than they have been in decades. We have the largest economy on the planet, and we don't have an unemployment rate that could bring down the global economy like the one that started in 2007.

Even as the government shutdown continues, our government was able to pass its fiscal year 2014 budget. According to a report, the U.S. government spent $1.2 billion during the federal shutdown.

Even more importantly, because the government shut down, Congress delayed its plans for raising taxes on the wealthy to avoid hitting the debt ceiling.

Of course, it still couldn't go on forever. As the Washington Post points out:

"Congressional leaders have agreed to a stopgap appropriations measure, but it includes a provision that blocks a new tax on high earners."

As of Monday afternoon, the measure was still holding up. And Congress could only afford to keep it open for as long as it takes for Congress to decide how to handle taxes.

In this post, I'll be taking a step back in time and talking about something most of you won't even know what to call it.

The term is commonly referred to as a "coupon", but it's not as simple as that. A "coupon" is a promotion that you can buy on a website or in a newspaper that can be redeemed at a later date with a specified reward or benefit, such as a coupon or rebate. The term itself usually means a promotion that expires after your current reward or benefit (with your own money, not from others' money), but does not always adhere to this definition. That being said, the first time you encounter the term, you probably think of "coupon."

But this post isn't about a "how to use a coupon" post. No, I'll be covering a whole lot more. I'm really curious to discuss the definition in more detail and why people use these discounts anyway. So let's put aside the nomenclature and get together some food for thought.

A History of Coupons and Promotions

In case you're unfamiliar with the term, "coupon" itself was coined in the United Kingdom in 1873 by William Alden, who was a journalist who wrote for a magazine. Originally, coupons were simply little notes that the seller distributed that he could turn into discounts on his merchandise.

In the early twentieth century, stores would have coupons on hand to mark down items or offer special promotions. This became so common that the New York Times did a story about the business of coupon.

The Times story said:

The coupons are sometimes used for anything from the purchase of a new pair of shoes with a twenty cent discount, to the purchase of a box of candy with a five hundred dollar discount. In fact, most people have a stock of coupons in the back of their pocket. They are available, in short, as part of one's business package.

Over the next few decades, "coupon" started creeping into everyday English, as we became used to seeing the term in the news or on a product package, in an effort to make it more generic. It was then that the term "coupon" got associated with discounts.

In 1954, a Washington Post writer began the "Coupon War" with that term in mind, writing on a coupon:

"Coupons have become a new and highly successful way of advertising and marketing goods, since they can be made up at the last minute and can be presented without a price."

This was followed up by a 1964 article in Reader's Digest. In it, George Laskas said:

"Coupons are a form of marketing."

It was then that "coupon" was used with some degree of frequency until the mid-1960s. However, despite the name, the "coupon" discount was often unrelated to the item or sale offered. It was a marketing phenomenon that eventually became the "coupon."

The Beginning of "Coupon"

In a 1954 post, "Coupon Wars", George Laskas said:

The term coupon actually comes from a combination of coupon and discount. The original one used was called a "coup" and had coupons printed in one-cent nickels with the price listed right under. They weren't too successful as a form of advertising since they didn't cost anybody anything to produce or deliver.

In 1964, the term "coupon" started to come up on the Web when someone named Mike Weltz wrote:

"Coupons" may be a contraction of "coupon" – and yes, I did come up with the term – but in my head it's the other way around.

In the same year, the United States Library of Congress did something that was really important at that time and that is called the American Printing House for the Blind (now known as the American Printing House for the Deaf). They published Manual Number 11: The Use of the Code C, which said:

The term "coupon," in English, literally means a coupon or discount. However, in our dictionary it is defined as a discount; it means "coupon" in French (coupon est dûment défâtissant, from dûment meaning to discount), in Spanish (cápiz en español, from the word cápiz meaning coupon), and in Italian (campa della valore, from valore meaning coupon, the word being used as an abbreviated form of the common Italian term "campa."

In the summer of 1854, George Frederick Hardie came up with a novel idea: a giant balloon. The idea would be revolutionary, of course, for when ballooning began, the only people who used them were scientists. But at the time, the idea seemed like insanity, according to our historians, because nothing of this scale had been attempted before.

Hardie, an engineer, knew that it would be possible to lift a man from the Earth's surface to an altitude of more than 100,000 feet without much difficulty. He planned to use "a heavy iron ball of about the size of a loaf plate, and a frame as lofty as the balloon is broad," his book, The Aerial Voyage to the Poles, reveals. The balloon, which would weigh roughly a small car, would be filled with a nitrogen gas that would keep the man inside the balloon at a comfortable temperature, about 95 degrees F., as long as the balloon remained intact.

Hardie made plans to go up to 60,000 feet, or nearly 200 miles, but died before he could successfully reach these altitudes. His wife would give up the project on the eve of one of his final test flights in New York, but she would eventually take the balloon to 60,000 feet and survive the flight intact.

This story seems to capture the mind of people pretty much anywhere, but what about the idea of a giant balloon? If you're a scientist or engineer, do you really think that you could pull this off with a balloon so large that it would easily encircle the Earth? And if you're a regular person, how would you get so far up into the skies?

A Huge Balloon Makes for a Really Big Balloon

In the 1840s, ballooning became more popular as more people started flocking to the countryside to get away from the heat of cities or from the threat of hurricanes. As demand for air travel rose, the first balloonists made their way to the American West. From there, the sport quickly became more popular outside the United States. From the 1880s through the 1930s, ballooning went international. Ballooning became a major sport in most of Europe and throughout Asia. In 1935, the balloon was introduced to North America.

If all this sounds a little more difficult than you think, don't despair. This big idea of a giant balloon was not all that crazy. Before his death, Albert A.E. Coster-Mullen, a renowned scientist and inventor, came up with a plan on how the weight of the balloon and structure of the balloon would be carried along by the air currents. Coster-Mullen's plan was an impressive one, particularly for its time, as he imagined constructing a giant balloon of some 45,000 feet in diameter with a diameter of 5 miles. As he explained in an 1897 patent application, his balloon would be made of a steel frame that would envelop the balloon's interior and would measure "sixteen and one-half feet high by the diameter of the balloon." The balloon would use a piston to act as its centre of gravity.

If this were the case, you might think that the weight of the balloon would keep its shape and the balloon would be very rigid. However, in the case of Coster-Mullen's plan, the weight of the balloon would come from the weight of the gas (and not of the individual humans inside) that was used to keep the capsule in place.

The air currents, Coster-Mullen reasoned, would not cause the balloon to float up off into the atmosphere — only the weight of the gas inside would make it rise. That would allow the balloon to break apart (it was designed to be airtight) and fall back to the ground.

So how big would a balloon have to be to make this work? Well, a balloon more than 80 feet in diameter would have been too large, and the dimensions of the balloon would be a little bigger but still below 60,000 feet. If a balloon more than 200 feet in diameter (about the length of a football field) were put together along the same lines, it could support the weight of a man.

How Far a Balloon Can Fly and Still Remain Alive

To keep the man in the balloon, you might think that it would need a lot of air and the air would have to be very, very thin. Well, it doesn't — and the human body is just that thin. According to one researcher, the amount of water that's in the human body is comparable to the volume of a soft drink bottle. So the balloon and the human inside it could keep on floating for a long time if an atmosphere of pure oxygen was used. According to this researcher, a good amount of nitrogen inside a balloon could also keep it afloat for a period of time if the balloon's centre of gravity remained on a balloon with the same diameter as one's body.

Darrell James Smith received a 23-month sentence by Judge Michael Zagel before the judge ordered him to pay $1.2 million in restitution to the Chase Bank. In September, Smith was also ordered to serve three years of probation.

On the first date, Smith appeared in court shackled and showed no emotion. On the second, Smith looked directly at the ceiling and spoke to Zagel after his name was called during his sentencing.

Zagel said, "No sentence is a good sentence for the person that committed the crimes against you. But it is a sentence as a deterrent for other people and as a deterrent for the public. That is all I ask, and I'm willing to move forward with that.

"I apologize, your honor. No offense," Smith said.

During the first two robberies, he took more than $1,000 from the two tellers. In another, his accomplice left his wallet behind, and, in the third, Smith walked out with $7,400 and credit cards.

After his release, Smith was described as an active member of his congregation. He was also a member at the Emanuel AME Church, and his wife was an intern at the Chicago Historical Museum.

Calls to both institutions went unanswered.

"If this is the future of what we do ... this has got to be bad for Canada," says NDP leader Tom Mulcair and the rest of New Democrats in response to news reports that Facebook, Twitter, Yahoo and other U.S. online services could be blocked in Canada as soon as Monday.

"The American companies who provide these services should be more than happy about it," said Mulcair (who, by the way, is Canadian).

For Canada's privacy commissioner, who's heading up an investigation into federal oversight of Canadian online spying by the U.S. National Security Agency, the latest developments are worrisome.

Monsef's office says it's not clear whether the NSA has access to "billions" of metadata online, but she says that the current "threat level" would require her immediate attention.

"My office has been asked to investigate this at the request of the prime minister and his public safety minister. We're going to find out as much as we can, and we'll report back on the findings of the investigation and our conclusion as we can," said Monsef's press secretary, Meghan Rickford.

In addition to Twitter and Facebook, the government faces pressure from public advocates to act, such as the ACLU and others, to ensure the Canadian Security Intelligence Service has more oversight or accountability and to create new legislation to rein in U.S. spying.

Other than the NSA news, Monsef and Rickford didn't say much in response to the Canadian press, except to say it has been the goal of the prime minister's communications team to bring the two nations closer together, and a meeting between Monsef and her Canadian counterpart Stephen Harper was the result.

"I think that, as a former minister of the justice, I'm always looking to develop those very important ties between our two countries," said Mulcair, who's also an adviser to one of the largest unions in Canada with more than 2.5 million members, known as Unifor. "I am hopeful that the prime minister and the minister for public safety and national security will continue to build ties with their American counterparts."

Twitter's Head of Public Policy, Sarah Harrison, declined to comment, referring requests to a press release the company put out on Thursday.

The company said it welcomes the recent steps taken by the Obama administration, including a bill (the USA Freedom Act) which is "unprecedented transparency legislation that would end the NSA's bulk metadata surveillance program, and end the NSA's bulk phone metadata surveillance program."

While it's hard to say whether Twitter won the PR battle with the NSA in the U.S. or has been forced to adapt to new security threats from other sources, "the American government clearly recognizes the risk that we are, as an organization, taking on as we grow," Harrison said in a statement sent to The Globe. "This is a major moment for our company."

For its part, Google made a similar statement that said the legislation "would be a major win for the privacy and security of our users around the world."

Even if Twitter and Google are forced to adapt, however, it's clear Canadians are paying attention.

"It's really going to be very interesting to see the reaction, the impact, in Canada, and, as important, the impact in the U.S.," says Rickford.

What's happened in Canada is happening worldwide, according to Twitter's top lawyer.

"This is not a Canadian issue anymore, it's a global issue," said Colin Crowell in an interview with Bloomberg. While Canadians have not been explicitly affected by U.S. spying, the company and other American service providers have faced public pressure to explain how their users' data could be used.

Canadian law doesn't require companies to disclose how their communications are actually retained or searched, which is troubling, says Crowell, who says Twitter will work with Canadian officials to respond to the new laws.

It's hard for me not to think of I Love Lucy when I hear about a "smart gun," but I have had a hard time finding any references to that beloved show. The idea of a futuristic gun that can only fire in the same direction it is pointed at sounds very like the one in "I Love Lucy," but a new proposal for such a firearm makes that idea sound almost plausible.

The idea of a "smart gun" has been around for a few years now, but it hasn't really been put into practice because the technology is relatively hard to use (see the video below where two children play with the technology). But this new proposal looks to be the first application of an RFID gun. It's so simple it's almost a joke (and one that I hope gets further developed and tested). But it's not really a joke. Because it could save lives.

Advertisement

The proposed smart gun is the world's first "smart" ammunition. I haven't had time to review the proposal yet, so it's possible I'm missing something important. But I'm guessing that a smart ammunition system would keep track of whether or not it's been fired, would only fire when needed, and would not fire if it's pointed toward an object that it is holding, such as a child.

That last bit is key. The idea is that the gun would work at the point of the gun rather than the gun itself. Because in one scenario if a toddler had picked up a loaded gun and accidentally shot someone, and then pointed the gun at her mother, the gun would fire with the same force (or close enough) that it did when it was just pointed at the child.

The proposal was created by researchers at the University of Pennsylvania and looks to be one of the first practical projects to implement the possibility. It is also fairly expensive, costing $25,000 to produce one firearm. So it may not be a viable option for all shooters. However, it could be a big win for the gun control community, as more and more Americans are learning how to use smartphones and other devices.

So what do you think? Would you buy a gun with this gun in it, or would it make you feel safer to hold your gun to your child's head? Or maybe we should all just stop holding guns to our kids' heads and just let them shoot each other!

In a country like Turkey where everyone speaks Kurdish, and is a member of a political party representing that language, why does it make anyone so mad if a group of Turks or Kurds want to celebrate Kurdish New Year?

Many argue that the current conflict between the Kurds and Turkey has little to do with Kurdish New Year. They say that the clashes and fighting only happen after the traditional Muslim "tayammum" season is over: the month-long celebration of "new" life starts in late February and runs through the summer and autumn. In Kurdish-populated areas, including Diyarbakir, and in Turkey, Kurdish-speaking locals may be the only one left in their families who is left-in-the-middle, but still participates in the festivities.

In fact, the reason the two groups have fought so much is not because of the Kurds' celebration of New Year but what it represents: a fight over what the Kurds are and who they are, and what they stand for.

Turkey claims that they are "terrorists", while the Kurds say that they represent a more diverse political position – for example, the Kurds are the largest ethnic group in Turkey outside of Istanbul without a place in politics, as well as the largest Kurdish population in Europe outside of their own country. This conflict has left behind an entire generation, and some even say entire generations, displaced.

It is this "new" Kurds (with an estimated 2,000,000 in all) that Turkey says are at war with it, while the Kurds, say they are the peaceful people standing up for their own rights. In fact, Turkey has been targeting the Kurds since 1974, when military leader Necmettin Erbakan's forces were trying to suppress the Kurdish uprising at Mt. Avcilar. As part of the Erbakan process Turkey forcibly displaced more than 1.5 million Kurds and created new areas for them in western Turkey. The Kurds became the targets of ethnic discrimination in the post-Erbakan era. For example, Turkey recently started a new Kurdish history course, which teaches the Turks and Kurds that their ancestors lived side by side and did not live a separate history. It also shows children a film about the Turkish-Kurdish war for independence (and a war, by Turkey's own logic, for peace).

Kurdish New Years: The Real Story is about why this year's celebrations might be more likely to be peaceful, rather than confrontational. It presents the main reasons for Turkish fears and why the Kurdish celebrations might be more likely to reflect the genuine spirit of this part of Turkey.

First and foremost is that Kurds are the largest ethnic group living in western Turkey without a place in politics

A second reason is that Kurds are the largest ethnic group in Turkey outside of Istanbul without a place in politics, and many of them are currently in asylum, such as the 700,000 refugees with a long history in Turkey. There are many important reasons why we do things the way we do on Earth, and they are not restricted to planetary and astronaut exploration. A huge number of biological and physical phenomena are affected by our planet's gravity, especially when we consider that some of these phenomena have an influence on our health.

1. The Earth creates tides.

Tides are powerful, slow-moving geological phenomena that occur throughout the Earth's oceans and on the continents. They usually occur when the Earth is tilted from a horizontal to a vertical position, called obliquity. On average, the Earth's gravity tilts the Earth about 2.5 degrees (or approximately 9.8 centimeters), but this varies greatly from one place to the next.

Because the surface of the Earth and oceans are the same solid substance, the Earth and the oceans are always in equilibrium. (The difference in densities of the two substances ensures that the equilibrium is maintained.) However, when we have a low-velocity wave traveling at high speed (such as when the Earth makes a turn), the force on the Earth's surface is a bit stronger, and this causes the ocean surface to "rise" up by about 20 centimeters (7.3 inches) every hour, as the wave moves through the water.

Every year, our oceans also rise by an average of 10 centimeters (4.5 inches) and every century, they rise by an average of 2 centimeters (0.8 inches). The Earth's gravitational pull is strong enough to make the ocean rise by an extra 2 centimeters every 24 hours if obliquity is tilted from 90 degrees to 270 degrees. That's why the North Atlantic has more water than it did 250 years ago. The water in the Mediterranean and the Pacific ocean get squeezed out by this process. For this reason, the United States is a net exporter of energy and a net importer of food. These are good reasons for why some people say that the Earth's tides are an important part of its character.

2. The planet's gravitational pull acts like a compass.

Another important aspect of a planet's gravity is that it produces a gravitational force that acts like a compass on our planet -- pointing us in the direction that the planet is taking us. This is a key feature of the geologic record, as the gravitational pull of the Moon can be seen over time. However, scientists have yet to fully identify how the Earth rotates, which accounts for its tilt.

Scientists believe that the Earth is tilted by about 13 degrees (see Figure 2). The tilt changes over time and is affected by many factors -- such as changes in the orbits of Mercury and Venus (see Figure 3), the orbital period of Jupiter and Saturn (see Figure 4) and the positions of our Moon and Sun with respect to Earth. For the last 2 1/4 million years, there has been no movement of the Earth's axis, which means that the Earth's axis has been tilted by around 12 degrees over the last 2 million years.


Source: NASA

We humans live on a tilted world, and because this tiltting is so important to our existence as beings that move around on a planet, it's a valuable thing to observe. The tilt also affects several important biological aspects of our lives -- for example, tidal cycles and the way seasonal winds affect human migration patterns.

3. The Earth holds the ocean in a position that makes it stable for life.

The Earth is the only planet in the Universe that houses a liquid and solid core and a solid mantle. It is also the only one of the four known planets to have water. The Earth itself is quite big -- about 300 times smaller than Earth's moon. However, water surrounds us at a surface pressure of only 3.4 tons per square meter (3.8 pounds per square inch). This is much lower than that of the oceans, which are denser and have a pressure of about 10,000 tons per square meter (10,300 pounds per square inch). Yet water remains stable at a lower pressure because it is a semi-solid (solid, but with a liquid outer liquid layer). In fact, it is the only solid material under the pressure of the surrounding liquid.

Because of its extreme density, water would sink if it was put on its side, but it wouldn't flow or move like a liquid. Water is also a liquid on Earth, and this enables it to "escape" and flow without friction through pipes and pipelines.

4. The Earth's gravitational field is why we feel gravity.

The gravitational force is the force exerted by an object over another object. In our Solar System, gravity is strong enough that spacecraft in low Earth orbit experience a force almost twice as strong as that of light. This is why we feel the Earth's gravitational pull when we look at it from below or from Earth.

In its final week before Election Day, Gov. Andrew Cuomo's State of the State Address includes a promise of spending $1 billion on affordable housing. But how much of that money will make its way into the hands of the residents of low-income Brooklyn?

There's the potential problem of a lack of local affordable housing in Manhattan compared to other places. But there could be even more trouble.

A recent study by N.Y.U.'s Furman Center found that the city's new affordable housing policy, which focuses on "priority" buildings, is disproportionately hitting "poor people," in fact, "about half of existing and new housing built is now in this category," according to Furman's Marc Berman, a member of the council for the Council on American-Islamic relations and co-author of the study.

"The goal is actually affordable for the most disadvantaged people," said David Rosen, the executive director of Furman. "But if your plan relies on prioritizing a building to the point where only the poor and poor-ish would be able to live there, suddenly all of this affordable housing is in jeopardy."

In one example, a study in the Furman report found that a "priority" housing building would have to demolish a three-story building in order to build more affordable housing, which meant the affordable housing that would go into the building would be smaller and therefore lower-paying. And it's these affordable units that the Furman report found aren't going to those who can least afford them.

The Furman study found that on the whole, the new affordable housing policy is hitting the poor more than the rich. Even if you look at just one type of building, like luxury apartments, where the cost of an apartment is low, "the income of higher-income renters is actually more likely to increase in the city than in the rest of the state," said Berman.

So when Gov. Cuomo says he's going to spend nearly $1 billion, what he truly means is he's going to spend it on the very thing that has driven up costs in the city's private markets. The Furman report's researchers found that on the whole, the new development policy is actually hitting the poor more than the rich. Even if you look at just one type of building, like luxury apartments, where the cost of an apartment is low, "the income of higher-income renters is actually more likely to increase in the city than in the rest of the state," said Berman.

"So it's not going to go towards improving the financial health of low-income people," says Rosen, referring to the policy's approach. "One of the main drivers to cost in the market is the demand on higher and higher income and therefore it will hurt those most in need."

Rosen says that in Manhattan, "as a rule" the new affordable apartments in the city are going to the very same folks where the state is trying to send a big chunk of that $1 billion in a state-wide approach to creating new affordable housing.

In a statement to Curbed, the governor's office said the plan would provide 100,000 permanent affordable apartments and "support thousands of additional units of affordable housing in other development projects across the five boroughs in the next decade." And that these funds should eventually be able "to fund the construction of new units of affordable housing in targeted areas."

The governor's office referred us to a statement from Housing and Urban Development Secretary and NYC Comptroller Scott Stringer, who also called for the state to use its "extraordinary resources" to "create new units for the needs of those in need."

"Today New York State is investing more than $400 million into affordable housing throughout the state in a single year. The Governor is committed to supporting the construction of affordable housing projects in the private market that will help New Yorkers reach their full rental potential," said Stringer's statement.

For Furman's Berman and Rosen, $1 billion isn't good enough to create more than 100,000 affordable apartments, so they'll be asking for $2 billion, which would generate enough new housing the Furman report calculates would be affordable for 25 percent of New Yorkers.

The following post is from Michael Hiltzik, a Bloomberg View columnist and the author of "Five myths about Obamacare."

Obamacare is being rewritten again.

On Feb. 10, President Obama delivered a speech from the Oval Office in which he called for "a simpler, more affordable [health care] system. It is based on two simple concepts: You get to keep your doctor; and when you get sick, you get treated fast and your health care costs get controlled." He pledged to pass such legislation "with or without Congress."

He said he would not seek a second term. "Now it is up to this Congress to fulfill its responsibility to do right by the American people,'' Obama said. "That's why I'm asking you to do it."

Two weeks later, on Feb. 29, the president signed an executive order creating a Health Benefit Exchange. The purpose of the E.O., in plain language, is to "establish exchange-based health insurance marketplaces" in each state that would include "enrollees in a Health Benefit Exchange who are able to qualify for a qualified health plan."

The E.O., in plain language, means that insurers could sell coverage on the federal exchanges but be barred from offering it in the state-based Exchanges that have failed.

After years of promise and a rocky start, here was the White House declaring that the federal exchange would do what it was never supposed to do: create a national market. The fact that it would not actually open on schedule has done nothing to slow down the Obama administration's political maneuvering.

This is a clear signal that some of the most controversial parts of the law will survive to be implemented: the mandate, subsidized coverage for individuals and employers, and the expansion of Medicaid under the new law. But it also provides a strong hint that the White House is considering rejiggering the rest of the program to make it simpler, more affordable and more generous.

"We're going to be doing a lot of things in this next year and beyond, as I've already said," Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius testified Thursday on Capitol Hill. Two years ago, the Supreme Court struck down the Defense of Marriage Act and made the United States a federal government that legally recognizes the legally sanctioned domestic same-sex unions of heterosexual couples.

But it wasn't until the court's DOMA decision in 2013 that the LGBT community began to make significant inroads in politics, gaining some support from the presidential candidates and gaining political leverage in the face of an increasingly conservative Republican Party.

A recent Pew Research poll suggests that this will be a short time before a majority of Republicans support same-sex marriage. At around 40 percent of Republicans, the Republican Party has a large enough majority to pass the issue through their own caucus.

For the first time, a majority of Americans support same-sex marriage. And for as many of us have grown accustomed to seeing the Republican Party shift to the left as they have, it's an opportunity for Democrats hoping to flip the House of Representatives and keep control of the Senate.

Let me be clear, Democrats should not be complacent. As conservative Democrats know, getting to 52 seats in the Senate would give them control of the full legislative body.

Yet Democrats have the electoral math to do just that. They would need to flip five Republican seats to win back the majority, and they currently lack only two Republican-held seats in states where a presidential race is likely. The biggest obstacle to Democrats flipping 10 or more seats is still states where a Democrat hasn't won an election in decades. But the math should change at some point.

The Democratic coalition is more diverse than you probably think.

Just before the Supreme Court's DOMA ruling, only 6 percent of Americans identified as Republican to about 50 percent Democrats, according to Gallup. Since then, though, both groups have changed somewhat.

About 4 in 10 Democrats identify as Democrats today, while just over half identify as Republicans. Even so, many Republican politicians still think they've found the key to winning elections by touting their "very conservative" voting records. For instance, Sen. While Rubio may be out of touch with many Republican voters these days, the idea that Republicans can win by promising to preserve some elements of their "base vote" is wrongheaded. Not only is GOP voters a much more diverse bloc than Democrats, but Republicans represent the most conservative segments of the electorate, and the electorate increasingly supports LGBT equality, too.

A recent Pew Research Center exit poll found that 62 percent of Hispanic voters and 64 percent of African Americans identify as Democrats to 35 percent for Republicans.

Moreover, while the 2012 exit poll shows more Republicans in Congress opposing same-sex marriage than supporting it (38 percent opposing compared to 28 percent supporting), that's nothing compared to the number of Democrats supporting it (70 percent versus 41 percent).

In 2012, the electorate was very diverse among racial groups, with a majority of women (53 percent), non-Hispanic whites (59 percent), Latinos (55 percent) and Asians (53 percent) voting for the Democratic Party. That's because the electorate is more diverse than some may realize.

The Democratic coalition is more diverse than you probably think.

Researchers say they have found the first ever direct evidence that viruses may kill or disable the immune system, thereby allowing viruses to become "immortal".

In studies led by Rui Ma, associate professor of clinical virology at Rice University School of Public Health, researchers found that a viral particle that could infect a mosquito could make normal human immune cells respond with inflammation in response, which in turn could affect the immune system - resulting in viral infections and a higher prevalence of viral infections later in life, the researchers report.

"We don't know if this is a general mechanism for immune compromise or if it's the cause of certain viral infections," Ma said. To address the issue, Ma's team is studying whether a different type of viral particle can trigger this response.

The research is published May 6 in the journal Scientific Reports.

Viruses can mutate and change shape, but the most common viral particle, the spherical and circular SARS coronavirus, looks quite similar to a bacteria. While bacteria have cell walls - the outer layers of cells - bacteria viruses are free-floating in their own fluid-filled chambers in cells with membrane-like proteins that protect cells from infection. The virus's structure is very small and the virus is unable to replicate, but it can be inhaled or absorbed by an animal and potentially react in the human body. Most human cases of infections result from direct contact with mucus or other organisms that carry bacteria or viruses.

"There's been a great deal of work that has looked at the impact of viruses that have the ability to interact with cellular proteins to alter cell function. However, this is the first study to show that a virus that interacts primarily with the cell membrane can have an impact on the activity of the cell," said Ma, who is the lead author on a paper titled "Inflammasome Deficiency Induces Prolonged Inflammatory Syndrome Immunodeficiency in a Mouse Model" and a coauthor on a paper titled "Injury to the Inflammatory Inflammasome by a Microbial Vector Is a Key Factor in Viral Infections and Progression."

In both studies, the researchers tested the toxicity of SARS particles to human immune cells. They found that viral particles impaired cellular function in SARS-infected mice while the animals continued receiving antibiotics or receiving other anti-viral treatments.

"In the SARS model, the viral particles are highly virulent. They can be asymptomatic and cause damage to tissue that is difficult to repair or can even cause tumors when they spread to the lungs or other parts of the body," Ma said. "It is quite remarkable that in these types of viral infection where the viral particles are so virulent, the immune cells adapt to them and the viruses can't persist."

Scientists have known for a while that certain immune cells, called macrophages, in the bloodstream are under attack by a number of viruses, including the herpes simplex viruses that cause cold sores, the human papillomavirus that causes cervical cancer, and enteroviruses that infect babies.

In the new study, the researchers looked at a virus, called V. cholerae, which is found in the gut of about 25 percent of people around the world, including people with celiac disease. They focused on mice infected with SARS or the mouse model of SARS that is more closely related to humans to determine if the virus was a major contributor to SARS lesions, the researchers said.

Specifically, they used SARS mice (which were not infected with SARS virus themselves) to investigate the immune system response to the SARS virus. SARS mice were treated with either antiviral drugs - aspirin or prednisone - or a drug to block inflammatory proteins called interleukin-1ra, or IL-1Ra, which are found in the immune system of humans after they are infected with a virus, the researchers said.

The researchers found that antiviral drugs or IL-1Ra blocked the inflammatory response to SARS in both animals, which suggested that the antiviral medication was not causing the damage to the immune system that they thought it was, the researchers said.

The team followed two groups of mice. One group of mice were fed antibiotics and then injected intravenously with human SARS virus that had been grown in a lab, and a second group of mice were not injected with SARS and were fed antibiotics, but were not treated with a viral infection themselves. The team found both SARS mouse groups had lesions in their lungs that had been triggered by SARS exposure. However, when the SARS mice were treated with anti-inflammatory drug, such as aspirin, the lung damage went away, the researchers said.

In all three mouse experiments, researchers found that the inflammation caused by viral infections affected immune system function but that cells stopped responding to signals from the inflammatory cells when the cells were removed or replaced

A little girl named Chloe is the star on this show as she has become a local celebrity. She has all the right people around her to help her, which includes an older sister named Madison, her friend and neighbor, Riley, and a love interest named Taylor. The series revolves around Chloe and her quest to be the best version of herself. She tries to deal with bullying, and her relationships among herself and her best friends. In spite of the show's title, Chloe is not the center of the story and only tangentially related to the other characters, so it doesn't get too far in terms of plot.


The character designs are a little unusual and sometimes cartoonish, as well. In addition, the soundtrack is not always original, with some generic songs that only add to the character of Chloe. As it turns out, this may sound like a small complaint to many, as the show works much better as a series that follows up and develops along with the plot. The show has its fair share of jokes, as well. But these are more in the form of short, humorous sketches, rather than the long jokes that we've gotten used to in recent years. However, Chloe's family also has a sense of humor, which helps make the jokes more enjoyable as opposed to the more sarcastic ones we've grown to get used to.


That being said, there are also some moments that may be difficult to enjoy. Despite the characters' efforts to make you laugh, the show has some really dark humor that may have viewers upset at certain points. This would be understandable if the show was set outside the normal family setting of the show, but the show is set within the small town of Tipton, Alabama, and that setting also features many issues and a lot of racism. This may not be the kind of show that someone would want to watch if they are sensitive to those sensitive subjects. Nonetheless, this is still only the first episode of the show, and some things may likely be addressed before the show reaches its full potential. But in the meantime, the show's quality seems to depend on the viewer's patience while waiting for the final four episodes.


One of the strengths of the show is that it isn't simply about character development, but is also about dealing with a lot of themes. While Chloe is dealing with her experiences and the problems facing her everyday life, many other issues are happening around her as well. This causes the plot to follow in the direction Chloe is going. This also has a tendency to make the show not about the characters directly. Instead, the characters in the show may try to act as stand-ins for Chloe as she deals with the issues in her life. For example, she often is the one who is forced to do things by Riley and the other friends. It's a nice way to bring some of the characters in an episode more to life for the viewer. For example, there's another person who also has a crush on Chloe, which adds more flavor to her friendship and their interaction with each other.


Overall, I really enjoyed the first season of Max and Chloe: The Movie and wish more shows would offer their audience more than just these two. But at the same time, this is a show that could be watched without any knowledge of the previous show, as it focuses on an entirely new storyline. This can serve to be an excellent show, depending on how much you are willing to invest in your experience. If you're the type of viewer who's looking for a well-crafted series where the plot and the characters are not as interesting as your own life, I think that you'll probably not like this show. For what it is, this is worth the watch.

It is common for people to describe a person as "sitting around doing nothing." Perhaps in our age of digital connectivity, with information readily available and endlessly connected to the most personal of details, what we do with our time now can be viewed not as a time of sitting but of "composing." Writing, or at least writing things down.

A recent study shows us that there are two sides to writing: creating and expressing. A recent study showed that creativity, on both an "active" and an "passive" level, can be cultivated out of sitting still: In a new survey of over 7,000 participants from across the world, researchers from Stanford and the University of Michigan found that writing more than 2 hours each day can lead to increased creativity. In fact, the benefits of a single day of regular writing far outmatched those of a week of exercise.

The first group of study participants took a writing challenge that involved creating a short story based on a real event, then reading it out loud to themselves over the course of a week. The latter group took a reading challenge that called for them to listen to a variety of recordings, then write them down. Both groups also took a test of creative thinking skills that asked them to think up 20 random words.

Overall, participants who wrote 2 to 9 hours each work day were about 10 percent more likely to score a spot on the creativity test than those who didn't write. For an average of 3.1 hours to write a new work of fiction, participants who wrote 2.5 hours each day scored an average of six points higher than those who wrote just 1.3 hours. And that's not even mentioning the additional time spent working on one's craft—research indicates the practice of taking breaks, rather than just working as part of an assembly line, can increase creativity and enhance creativity itself.

Advertisement

Other research shows that working a large group creates the same increase in creativity even if a person begins the task with the knowledge that their efforts will be limited. The new Stanford study, published in the Science journal, showed the same for people from all over the globe.

"Writing and speaking with someone other than in your own presence has a very strong link with creativity," said Prof. David Weinberger, a professor at the University of Michigan and one of the researchers involved. These results suggest that the activity of creating and listening and writing have a stronger link than the other ways of interacting with people. "The more that people interact with people, the more they interact with ideas that they take on to be their own ideas," Weinberger said in a press release.

So, what's more creative? If you're working that little bit harder, or just take some time to catch up on your writing, make sure to leave the rest of your day well spent.

The stadium issue is the biggest issue in the NFL. It needs to be resolved. We have heard it many times from the Ravens organization. We have heard it from the Eagles, Bills, Giants, and Redskins. We need a deal in place.

There are a lot of different ways you could approach the stadium issue, and they all present their own set of concerns. We need a way to resolve it in an acceptable way that is fair to the league.

We've been hearing more and more from those of us who live in Baltimore.

The city will not be charged for the stadium as long as the deal is done and the money is allocated appropriately by the state of Maryland.

The stadium is a must-win for the region and for America. We will have the new stadium of our dreams and the opportunity for our team to continue to thrive and compete on the national stage. Those are great things, but we can't forget about the city of Baltimore, which has put so much work into making the city a place where people can actually build something. It's a wonderful thing to get to that point, but now we need a team and the city needs some money for its infrastructure... a new stadium is key to the long term sustainability of Baltimore.

We have been assured that at least half will be privately financed. If the stadium is privately funded, it's the right thing to do.

We know it's a difficult issue in Baltimore.

There are two sides to the issue. On one side, there is a local effort that is looking for a deal that will allow the citizens of Baltimore to have a stadium of their own, for their team. On the other side, the city and team is looking for an agreement that will ensure that we have a fair deal for Baltimore -- the same deal as was agreed to by the NFL.

We've been very impressed with the way the Ravens have handled this and it has been very easy for us to work with the Ravens to get a very fair deal for Baltimore and get back to the work that is the foundation of Baltimore's future.

We are very encouraged to see how quickly the parties involved seem to be moving to resolve this issue.

The most crucial part of the stadium issue -- the one we are all focused on here -- is to make sure that a stadium is built that will have a long term positive impact on the city.

The stadium is the critical factor; the Ravens are working diligently to make sure we get this right.

On Tuesday, the NFL's owners will meet and decide what to do next with a stadium proposal in St. Louis. I'm confident that the Ravens and a few other teams will be able to bring something back to the table that will address any lingering concerns and allow for meaningful progress to be made on a stadium plan for Baltimore. We cannot and will not compromise on the important goals at this meeting. We will not sit idly by while a plan that has long been accepted and agreed upon by the stakeholders does not get built.

After working for four years to do something very important and positive for our city, the Baltimore Ravens have made it clear: We're ready to move forward with a plan that can produce a stadium for Baltimore that will not only produce a strong economic benefit for our city but also be a model for the NFL to follow.

For those who have been concerned or disappointed, we have a simple message. This is the time to move forward.

In the first of our two-part series on the state of the economy in Australia, we examine what the government wants Australia's banks to do — and how much will it spend. On the second of our two-part series, we consider the impact of government austerity.

The Reserve Bank of Australia has just released its quarterly Economic and Fiscal Monitor. Its most interesting finding comes in its analysis of the state of the national economy. A key point is its warning of an imminent fiscal crisis.

It is true that over the last three years, the government has pursued fiscal stimulus — spending more money. The stimulus was mostly undertaken by the states and the federal government, at the expense of the private sector, especially the banks. There was no serious attempt to rebalance the economy to make it more efficient.

So, while there was austerity at the federal level and a mild recession in Australia (the economy shrank 0.2 per cent in real terms between 2010-11 and 2011-12), there had been a large fiscal stimulus, not unlike in the US, if not actually bigger. The economy was growing quite nicely, before the recent drop in resource prices and the recent slump in global demand.

Of course, most economists don't think that Australia's problems are down to a "fiscal crisis". The crisis is a result of a structural problem in the economy — namely that too much private debt is being held at negative real interest rates, and the "recovery" hasn't worked as promised.

The key point about this episode is that it is unlikely to be repeated. In addition to the recent drop in commodity prices, there are good reasons why the public sector is unlikely to be required to pursue large-scale fiscal stimulus.

The government can only raise taxes. While there are some tax cuts to the mining corporations, to say nothing of the cuts to the GST, the budget remains constrained by the political imperative to raise revenue. To spend more would, according to John Daley, a former Banker, be a "political recipe for a fiscal catastrophe".

The Australian economy needs big-ticket stimulus spending

There are two ways of supporting the economy. The first is through infrastructure spending, which can be done either by the state governments themselves, and in addition, through public funding. An example of a stimulus that could be undertaken in this direction would be spending on airports, roads, ports, and other major capital projects in cities, in addition to increased levels of public spending.

The second way of supporting the economy is by stimulating consumption and investment in productive capacity, and providing jobs through public-sector employment programs. One important example is the Australian Workforce Investment Program — which includes job creation and apprenticeship training programs.

There are limits to how much this type of activity will produce demand from the private sector in the short term, yet it has a high impact in terms of employment and growth. It also is an effective mechanism to deliver a larger-scale fiscal stimulus than was done during the financial crisis, and a stimulus with lower rates of inflation.

The government in Australia can only do one thing — and that is spend. If it wants Australia to grow, then there is only one thing it can do: spend. With an ageing population and not enough working-age people to drive the economy, the government would be crazy not to seek to have an ageing population in Australia. And it has the power to do so through the welfare system, and through investing in public goods by the Australian government, such as infrastructure.

The private sector has many problems: it is, in many cases, poorly funded, undercapitalised and exposed to the risks of high unemployment and financial turbulence. In contrast, government can invest in infrastructure to create jobs and productivity, and provide pensions and health care coverage for working-age Australians.

Austerity is not the solution

The government's budget deficit figures have recently been revised downwards to $32.4 billion for 2011-12, after the budget was delayed by the Senate. In addition, there is the possibility that Australia's budget will actually be slightly better next year, and there is the potential for growth to accelerate. But there is no reason to think that the deficit issue — at current levels — is the only problem in Australia's economy.

The problems are structural and, as such, are unlikely to be alleviated by additional fiscal stimulus — if any such stimulus is implemented.

In Australia, it makes no sense to pursue a "stabilisation policy". Instead, it is much better for governments to pursue a policy of fiscal stability.

The first policy, fiscal stability, involves stabilising public debt. The public sector is responsible for about 70 per cent of all debt held by the private sector.
