As a kid growing up in northern California, a young George W. Bush was mesmerized and fascinated by George Orwell's 1984.

"I used to think it was all a little too idealistic and utopian," he told The Daily Caller. "Now I think it's totally realistic."

But even in 1984 there was a war on, a war on drugs that was raging in the 1980s, one that still continues today.

To this day, it is illegal to grow, sell or possess marijuana in the U.S. — not even for medical purposes.

The U.S. is the only nation in the world that has such laws.

And, for good measure, the Bush presidency made illegal all drugs from within his own country — something that had not occurred since the days of the American Revolution and the Whiskey Rebellion.

And, if you think that isn't bad enough, there's even more:

Bush is so obsessed with stopping the war on drugs that he is even threatening to withhold funding for the Mexican and Colombian governments if they don't crack down and begin cracking down on drug cartels who continue to send drugs into the United States.

Bush insists that drugs are the greatest threat to our society and that we need to stop them at its root, "and the root of the problem will always be prohibition."

You would think that in today's more enlightened times, someone with a higher voice and a more eloquent speech could have told the kids in 1984 about the real life consequences of those things that they all took so seriously.

Instead, we live in a world governed by this president who believes that we should enforce the drug laws in the same way that we enforce any law that has anything to do with women.

And what's worse is that this President is so adamant about not taking a hard stance on drugs that he will go so far as to order the execution of people who do nothing except grow and sell marijuana.

Bush would order the execution of a woman who has been to rehab to fight her addiction — when she was ready — and then she would be murdered so a new generation of addicts can continue to grow and sell the drugs that destroyed her. She would be murdered because she couldn't stop, and that's what is the most tragic and awful part.

But she can't stop, because nobody could stop it. Not President Bush. Not the drug police. The president's war on drugs is based on a lie.

These people are criminals who have ruined our lives, and Bush refuses to punish and imprison them for it.

The question is, why?

George Bush would like you to believe that we ought to turn our backs on the war on drugs that took us to a place where the most dangerous drug is still marijuana, and he would love to arrest and kill all of those people.

To this end, we're going to spend the next year taking a hard look at George Bush's legacy and what we have and what we don't know.

There have been a lot of articles written in the last week discussing the recent announcement from Google that they are taking their Android Pay mobile payment system to iOS and other platforms. With Apple already launching Apple Pay, and other companies, including AT&T and Walmart, also testing it around the country, the topic is an interesting one for the mobile payments industry. In today's article, we are going take a look at the latest in mobile technology for both iPhone and Android devices. In short, Apple Pay is set to launch with iOS 9.3, and we are going to take a look at the new functionality from a security standpoint.

Apple Pay has been on one hand, a big improvement over the previous payment systems available for smartphones. Android Pay is much more of a wallet based solution where you only get one credit or debit card with it. In contrast, Apple Pay allows you to have multiple cards, and even lets you use your phone as a PIN or password security device.

With Apple Pay, all you need is your fingerprint to make a purchase. However, with a new release from Google Wallet, Android Pay and Apple Pay have a few differences. First, Android Pay is no longer a "wallet only" system, but a system that integrates with every platform and payment app out there, similar to PayPal. There is no longer an option to use your fingerprint to make a payment – you just use the phone or tablet to make it at point of purchase. This allows your Android device to become a point of purchase and wallet when using Google Pay.

On the other hand, Apple Pay uses the Apple Pay app which lets you make payment transactions in your iOS device or iPhone. This makes the Apple Pay system extremely cross platform. Apple Pay has been available since the launch of iOS 8.1.1 and has been downloaded more than 8 million times. We have not used a single bank or financial institution using this technology, but it has been used by dozens of big retailers. In short, the new iOS 9.3 is making its way to the iPhone and now that we have used it for about a week, we are very impressed.

First, we were impressed with the stability of Apple Pay and the ease with which you can get through the transactions. When we went to make a purchase at a new restaurant, we were greeted with a "Congratulations! You're the first person to try Apple Pay!" sign up in the app. No more signing up for all the new financial institutions you want. Just give it a try and you will be very happy with the new Apple Pay experience. The only gripe we had during testing was the fact that it was harder to add new cards with Apple Pay, especially for the older iPhones that are out there.

On the other hand, you can imagine that Android Pay is a much more intuitive system. To make that purchase, just scan the fingerprint on the device and you are done. The downside for Android Pay is that Android phones have a slower processor compared to iOS and you may experience lag with it. We also noticed that Google still requires payment information to be entered manually from your device – it is not as simple as Apple Pay. That being said, we have had an amazing experience using Android Pay and we are definitely going to continue to use it once it launches on iPhone and all major Android operating systems.

This new innovation from Google has been a success and all major banks are already using it. The banks and payment systems that support Android Pay include Bank of America, Chase, Wells Fargo, Citi, American Express, U.S. Bank, Barclay Card, BBVA Compass, UnionBank, BMO Financial Group, PNC, Capital One, Chase, TD Bank, National Bank and Western Union.

It may not seem like much, but I think it is fair to say that Android Pay will be a major step in the mobile payments industry. It is not a new payment system that is not yet being implemented by multiple networks in the world, but it makes more sense for consumers to use something like Android Pay than a different payment solution like Apple Pay.

I would like to close this by stating, however, that this technology is not perfect. If you use Android Pay and go to an Apple store, you will still have to use a different payment terminal to make a purchase. Also, this technology is not yet available in stores all over the world. The technology still requires an NFC, contactless technology like the one supported by the iPhone and iPad to work. It will likely take a lot of companies and banks partnering together to complete the mobile payment revolution and that is something that we will have to wait and see.

Also, we have reached out to Google and had a chance to try out the new payment system. The response we received was nothing short of "we will let you know when Android Pay launches."

The government in Brussels is poised to pass a bill legalizing the production of weed for medical and recreational use. The EU's drug agency, the Commission, proposed the bill in February.

The proposal is not expected to be voted on until June, but it is already attracting opposition.

At least 26 MEPs in the European Parliament have spoken out against the bill, according to the Daily Mirror. This includes a group of doctors, medical patients, and anti-smoking lobbies.

"It is unacceptable and unacceptable that a legal substance, already prohibited by law in many EU member states, will be permitted for the first time in the 28-nation bloc," David Marshall, head of the British Medical Association's national body, said in January.

"This legislation will increase risks of addiction and abuse, increase the risks for the individual user and the community, and undermine international efforts to address drug dependency."

"A good proportion of the population will not appreciate the positive and beneficial aspects of decriminalization. As such we can expect a very strong resistance to this," MEP Christian Engström said to the Daily Mirror.

"It's about saving people money on police work, it's about saving money for the hospitals with these medicines," he added.

In the past few episodes, we've talked with a lot of people who have gone through the "sheltering life," or have made it to a certain distance of "normal". It seems as though these people know that normal exists. They know that it is possible to get in "a room" with another human being. They just need to realize that not every person they meet is that different from the people in the "sheltered life."

For example, one of our friends has been an out-and-proud atheist for some time. He gets to meet a lot of people of varying degrees of spirituality. Sometimes the religious people seem really nice for a minute - they act as if they're genuinely interested in him, not just as a fellow believer - he finds this encouraging. Other times, he just runs into people who have "the light" on their shoulders. While the latter are certainly more fun because they seem to be having a good time, sometimes the "light" (like being an atheist) turns him into a walking target. He can't help but notice this every time he sees a religion-related sign, or a prayer-related building, and the more he recognizes that, the less he feels like he has to keep going to a place of comfort.

But this brings us to another interesting point: Why is it so hard to leave the "sheltered life"? Why can no one just "snapoutofit" when faced with "religious nonsense"? It seems like many of these atheists (and freethinkers) have been in this bubble with their friends and family for a very very long time. They are still in that same position, only they've left the "sheltered life" behind. But as we are constantly told, "The more you love someone, the more they love you back". If you think this is true, then you don't really know what love is, do you? I think the point is this: If I was in that situation, it could potentially be devastating to be forced to leave someone you love. To me, leaving something you love is a kind of suicide. The thing that really makes it hard to leave the "sheltered life" is that the people who go through their "shelter" are the ones who have been through "survivors life". They are the ones like me who started their lives with a religious upbringing and who have grown up thinking that atheism was "evil".

What could be a better "escape" or a better "escape to God?" Could this even be possible? This makes me think of something that Jesus himself said. When the Pharisees were debating some issues (like Jesus was a murderer and therefore a blasphemer of God), Jesus replied: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God". When you find yourself in an environment, where every other person is a complete idiot, and you are perfectly content and happy, then you can have a very real possibility of finding salvation without needing to escape. You just need to be willing to accept Jesus at the cross when he appears. He is not there to help you out. He will show you the way if you let on to him, and he is the only way.

It is a weird thing to say that this is all a product of "cultural appropriation". A thing that can be said if someone is white, but to a nonwhite person who is raised in this culture, this is a part of how they "learn" about religion for example. In that situation, the white person might hear "It's OK if it's not white! Everyone's a little weird! If we are all the same and we find it impossible to do anything else, then let us just stay here". It is a very strange thing to say. But it is still a true thing. The truth is that we are ALL the same. There is no god or deity that is greater than the God that loves us with all of his heart, and that loves us to the point of death for us. Not every believer is going to have this kind of experience, but I think it is reasonable to say that the majority of believers don't.

There is no "god", and there is no afterlife. The "sheltered life" is just another part of life. And we don't even have to be happy. We just have to be open - and have the courage to take a few steps.

The White House has the luxury of spending a couple months looking at the results of the campaign without anyone having to look at the results of the campaign. You know who doesn't? The people who didn't vote. (The only time you ever see a poll about who voted or who didn't is in news articles about how your favorite candidate won.)

Donald Trump.

If the election campaign was a reality show, the last episode of the season would have been about how this election is going to affect Donald Trump's life in the months to come.

The first episode of the election in America is about Trump's campaign, the consequences of winning, and the way it will effect the next eight years of his life—and your personal life. The second episode is about the effects of losing a presidential election.

You may not have been able to watch those episodes all at once, given how early they aired. But you can watch them all in one fell swoop during the past 10 years.

All the information in these reports, which are being collected and compiled by The Fix for the Huffington Post, was gathered from publicly available records or data. These reports take a variety of different methods in order to come up with what we believe to be the most accurate information about American politics.

But don't take our word for it. Here are some of the experts who told us they believe they have the most complete picture of what is going on in American politics today:

Donald Trump

Donald Trump doesn't like polls.

"There's nothing in politics more interesting than politics and polls," Trump said in June. "Every poll is fake."

Pollsters, of course, were not always calling Trump's numbers "fake." In fact, Gallup's daily tracking poll of the race for the Republican nomination got Trump up to 36 percent in May. In the most recent poll, conducted Jan. 7-10, Trump received 42 percent to Ted Cruz's 36, Marco Rubio's 4 and Jeb Bush's 2.

But if he does in fact lose the election, he won't feel too much pain. In fact, Trump might get some more help.

In July, NBC News reported Trump's team had "begun planning an extensive media campaign designed to counter negative press coverage."

Trump's team already has a few options. "They have a media strategy. But they're still in the learning phase," one unnamed Trump aide told NBC.

For example, the president-elect plans to continue to visit places he's visited in the past—both for business and for campaign appearances—while the media focuses on the bad news.

CNN reported Trump would be making a surprise appearance at a meeting of technology and media executives scheduled for Sept. 13. That meeting is expected to include some of the media outlets that criticized him throughout the campaign.

One media executive said it would be in keeping with Trump's reputation. "No one is going to question the way that he's going to conduct himself or the agenda to which he plans to move his administration," said Steven Connolly, president of the Association of Press Journalists.

What is the purpose of our blog?

We're a small team based in London, UK. We created the blog as a place for our readers who love food and the world of healthy, vegan eateries. We hope you enjoy reading about interesting vegan food destinations around the UK and the world.

What do you think of the site? Do you think we have a good food blog?

This is our first ever blog (well, of course it was), so it definitely isn't as thorough as we would like it to be, but we are committed to adding to the site as we go along.

What's your favourite local vegan place?

This is a hard one. The truth is that our favourite local vegan foods are usually quite varied, and vary every single day. It's quite tricky to pick one favourite.

We are a huge fan of this place in the West End of London. It's a tiny place with a huge menu of vegetarian and vegan food, that also serves pasta. They've got everything from soup, curry, pizza, nachos to salads, pizzas, pasta, calzones and veggie ice cream. It's a bit of a pain in the neck coming here, but it's worth it when you try their vegan pizza. The staff are so nice and so knowledgeable. The atmosphere is lovely too and makes it feel more like a café than a restaurant.

A vegan bakery called Kale and Soul is another amazing place that has a big menu of vegan baked goods that are also available at the bakery. We got to know them when we visited and loved their baked goods.

You can also find vegan options in pubs. If you have a pint, you can get a vegan cheese ball from Vegan Pies (which is our favourite pub in London) or if you need a veggie milkshake, try Vegan Pies. They've got a number of vegan milkshakes and are usually pretty good.

Our favourite vegan restaurant

So this one really is a no-brainer. A vegan restaurant we love in London! It's such a cool place – the decor is pretty unique, with colourful lighting, and they cater for a wide variety of people. It has a really friendly atmosphere and is popular with students.

We spent a lot of time at this local vegan restaurant and it was the only restaurant to offer our entire group table service in the whole pub. It was really nice for everyone to sit down in a nice quiet area and talk to each other. The server, Dan, made us feel at home right from the start.

They only had the one vegan food item on the menu but each table ordered different things to sample. We got a dish with chickpeas, mushrooms, potatoes, rice and lentils on the side, and a veggie burger, as well as various salads. We even got a vegan quiche and cake to enjoy – they were tasty!

It was also really nice to have the option to go from table service to sitting on a deck area to watching the live soccer matches they play on a massive screen. The people who were eating there were definitely enjoying themselves, and the atmosphere was fantastic!

What's next for us? How should we grow?

We're a team of two people at the moment, so we're always looking for new people to help us grow. As our site gets more popular, so will the number of different posts we put on it. We'll also have more videos of people eating vegan and sharing their experiences on the blog.

We're also looking to expand to other countries, so if you live in one of them, please head over and subscribe to our newsletter!

The idea that some individuals can't be trusted with firearms is the reason it's illegal to carry a gun in certain places.

But a new federal court ruling raises the possibility that it could also be illegal to own one.

The ruling came Monday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia in a case involving a woman who bought a gun to defend herself against an intruder in her home in Rockville, Maryland. A judge refused to let her keep the gun, ruling that it violated a law banning felons from possessing firearms.

In this October 4, 2012, photo, a handgun is displayed at a firing range near Fort Monroe, Va. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

The law applies only to convicted felons, not to the more than 300,000 Americans who are prohibited from owning guns because they have committed crimes that put them beyond the protections of background checks and other regulations. And gun rights activists say the government's ruling means, for the first time since the Second Amendment was adopted in 1791, that federal law doesn't restrict gun ownership.

"I think it's a monumental victory for our clients," said John Malcolm, assistant legal director at the Second Amendment Foundation, a group that has advocated for gun rights. "This has never been a good day to hold up the Second Amendment."

[Related: 'Gun owner'? Not so fast]

The case is a rare instance of a case being decided in the lower federal courts when the issue will actually be enforced. The lower court ruling came in an appeal filed against a federal magistrate judge who ruled in October 2011 that the woman had to sell her gun under a "prohibited" category of the National Firearms Act.

The woman's attorney asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit to rule in her favor instead of letting the gun remain under the federal law that defines who can have a gun. A unanimous panel of judges at the appeals court refused. In order to have his gun kept as a state property, the attorney would have to turn it over to state officials "as soon as practicable."

Gun control advocates worry that the decision leaves a lot of guns, including assault rifles, unprotected and could allow individuals to keep them in their homes. But the ruling is unlikely to impact any of the approximately 40 million guns owned by Americans.

"The decision in [the D.C. Circuit ruling] is an anomaly," Malcolm said. "We are very pleased that the decision is limited to a case of a single gun owner who did not ask for the government's permission to keep their gun for defensive purposes. The fact that this doesn't affect the rights of every gun owner in the country makes it a good one."

[Related: Gun control groups appeal for gun rights to go on equal footing]

The case involves a woman, whose name is being withheld to prevent identifying her, who bought a Sig Sauer pistol in 2012 to defend herself and her family against an intruder. She had been legally prohibited from possessing a gun for 10 years.

When she heard her dog was barking out of a bedroom window the night she made the purchase, she got a gun and went outside. When she looked through the peephole she saw a man looking into her bedroom. She shot twice, hitting the man in both legs and stopping the intruder. Because she shot the intruder, the case is still open and she has not been charged.

A judge told the woman that because she had previously been convicted of a felony and now had an illegal gun, she could not possess the weapon legally. According to the D.C. court decision, the woman argued that she was protected by the Second Amendment because of her being a convicted felon that could have been prevented by the law. But a different federal court panel disagreed.

"The Second Amendment, we maintain, does not protect a criminal defendant who is not prohibited by state law from possessing firearms," wrote Judge Frederick S. Scullin Jr. in the October opinion.

"For nearly two centuries, the Second Amendment's central promise: 'A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the Right of the People to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed,'" Scullin continued, "has been recognized as an essential element of any scheme to render the national militia effective."

Pablo Neruda wrote about the "fairy tale of a great man and his little woman," and that's pretty true of the life of Pablo Neruda. The Colombian painter, who is famous for some of his very long paintings, wrote in one of the texts that he was a fan of his mother's favorite author, Miguel de Unamuno, and would often read her books.

It's possible that the love affair began when Unamuno was working as a teacher; at the age of 12, he was on a trip to Paris to teach. One day while walking around the city, "He came upon some poor boy and began teaching him Spanish, and taught him the rudiments of it, as well as the history of the country. As it was impossible that, in a country which was only about half Spanish, he should forget his native language for so long a time," Neruda wrote.

It's hard to say how the relationship really developed, considering it's hard to find any proof. When Neruda was a little boy, his father died; as a result, his mother's health declined and she was constantly hospitalized. Because his parents had moved to Colombia for his mother's care, there was no one, besides himself, who could take care of the house and the farm. Neruda's mother's closest friend was his neighbor, Manuel de Landa (known as Manolo).

One day, when Manolo was on his way to work, Neruda's mother picked up a small parcel. It was from Manolo and contained a letter. The letter was from Miguel de Unamuno. Neruda read it.

It was the first time Manolo wrote him; Neruda read the letter, which was about Unamuno's love of Pablo Neruda and how Unamuno felt that Neruda should be honored for his writing. The two wrote that Unamuno appreciated Neruda's love of poetry, and felt that he should be celebrated.

As they continued to talk, Neruda began to love Unamuno all over again. "I, Pablo Neruda, write to you with an intense feeling of delight and love, that I am your son," the letter read. "When you wrote to me, I did not know whether I would be able to endure. And when I read your letter, and discovered the true greatness of your language, I found it impossible to stay at home, to wait patiently for that great book of yours … I have loved you every instant of its being read and I have long loved you ever more intensely, knowing that when it becomes known to all the world, I shall have been found wanting, as no one has, no one other than you has ever been found wanting."

Manolo then went on to say that Neruda was "much too far advanced in his studies to understand your message." But Neruda wrote back to say that he understood his message.

In addition to writing about his love for his wife, Neruda also became something of a writer himself. He published two novels: "El Nariz" and "Manolo," which are about love and sacrifice in the Spanish Civil War.

"What does the Bible teach about eating animals?" I heard that question for years by myself and it always perplexed me. My understanding of the Bible was only as good as the version of its story I learned as a kid. It was only through the Internet that I could start learning more. Since that time I became an advocate for meat-eating in general. I was not alone in that and a good number of Christians in America became vegan as a direct result of learning about the Bible. For those who are a bit more knowledgeable of Biblical principles, it is clear that Scripture provides ample insight as to the proper way to use animals and their products. This is the heart of what the Bible teaches about animal use:

1- God created the animals on the fourth day, not as in modern times with modern technology.

2- God's purpose was to be merciful before creating them for food, as a reminder to His people of His love for them.

3- God did not create the animals with the intent of using them for food.

4- Animals were intended to be our food, and we should treat them as such.

5- The purpose of eating animal flesh and eating its meat products is to honor God by eating a living sacrifice made in His name.

God created Adam and Eve as a reminder for His people to be holy creatures and to not desecrate God's name. If God is our holy idol, then to desecrate Him we must desecrate His image.

6- The Bible tells us that God gave man dominion over the plants, which is the reason we created all the animals.

7- Even in our modern times, plants are the most intelligent of all living creatures. We can make them do all of the things we want with them.

8- Animal flesh and animal products have become our most valuable commodity and are used as our first line of defense against disease and predators.

9- God will eventually allow us to eat animals, at least for a small period of time. Then, it will be time to make more sacrifices from our most loved ones. Then, it will be time to start eating animals in their natural habitats.

10- It was not God's intent to allow us to make animals into our slave labor of labor.

11- Even though God created our bodies as male and female, we can still make a covenant with God and change our sex. Our bodies are our best gift to God, and if we choose to use them to be a gift to others God will bless us with more than we could ever have imagined.

The following article is a guest post by Dr. Scott Gottlieb, Chairman of the FDA's Prescription Drug Advisory Committee, and his colleagues, Dr. David Kessler, Dr. Andrew W. Ullman, and Dr. John P. Wood, and Dr. Michael M. Wood, Ph.D.

It is no easy task to get a new prescription drug approved by the FDA. Approval represents just one step—one step that typically means the drug will be sold to hundreds of thousands of Americans and will change the way we live, work, and play—and many Americans who use prescription drugs are eager for these benefits.

But what about those without health insurance and those without a prescription? Are those people likely to benefit from a new prescription drug, and, if so, how many benefits do we need before we approve a drug?

Recently, the FDA approved the first new drug since the enactment of President Obama's Affordable Care Act (ACA), the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, for use by non-elderly Americans. As with any new drug, the impact of this drug is uncertain, but in the words of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the new drug "is a significant milestone, providing patients with treatment for people in need. The FDA approval is a good step for patients who need these treatments, and it should lead to increased access to these therapies."

I'm very interested in learning more about the cost-effectiveness of the new drug, a topic that often comes up as the cost of medications, medical technologies, and other health care delivery services comes under increased scrutiny. A recent study published in the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) analyzed the cost of treating one of the three patient populations, as well as non-covered patients and the uninsured, for 14 new, FDA-approved drugs approved for use between 2004 and 2011 [1,2]. The NEJM estimates that the new drugs were expected to bring about a cost savings of more than $9 billion by the year 2020, when some of the drugs will be available for general prescription use.

While the NEJM study didn't account for the additional cost of the FDA approval process and the cost of marketing a new drug, it is important to remember that the cost will be passed onto individuals through higher prices when pharmaceutical companies charge for medications, and by higher out-of-pocket costs.

The authors also found that for new drugs that are not in the top half of new drugs that were approved between 2004 and 2011, the median cost was almost $4,000 per patient. Of the top 15 drugs, the median cost of treatment was $13,100 per person. For some drugs, the median cost was up to nearly $200,000 per person, with the median cost being almost $7 million per year per patient. These drug costs far exceed the $800 or $1,000 per year it costs to treat each patient in the "typical" health insurance plan—$1,600 for an individual and about $5,400 per family, depending on the plan. And, these costs also far exceed what people are typically able to obtain through insurance companies.

As the authors note, one important cost concern is the high cost of marketing drugs. Marketing costs account for about 25 percent of a drug's price and have risen even faster than the overall medical price inflation over the past five years. According to the study, about 75 percent of the drugs had advertising costs, and these costs have risen faster than the overall medical inflation.

There is one other potential cost concern—which is why some new drugs are so expensive—for patients who are uninsured. To address this concern, as mentioned above, we may want to wait for more data on the cost of this drug rather than allowing those without health insurance access. As for non-covered patients, many may not receive coverage, and it seems likely that such a drug would be subject to the same advertising and marketing concerns as the drugs that are covered. For example, the authors of the NEJM study have noted that, "[i]n 2006, the number of drug-covered hospitalizations fell to 6.3 million (down 8 percent from 2006), and in 2012, that number was down to 5.0 million (down 31 percent from 2006)." It is likely that these number will only increase over the years to come and those without coverage will not receive coverage for this drug.

I have been working on a long-term study to assess the cost benefit of Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries who benefit from the new Medicare prescription drug benefit. The goal is for this data to enable us to estimate the cost benefit of a new drug to Medicare beneficiaries based on the cost-benefit formula for all drugs and the benefit-cost ratio for Medicare Part D and Part B drugs.

Over the next several months, I will publish a series of articles on this topic and work with the authors of the NEJM study on developing a more precise calculation

LIMA (Reuters) - Peru will make $200 million available to the United States and other Western nations involved in the South American free trade area, President Pedro Pablo Kuczynski said.

A sign is seen at the entrance of the Peruvian free trade zone before the signing ceremony in Lima, Peru January 27, 2017. REUTERS/Mariana Bazo

He made the announcement on Friday in Lima amid growing pressure from the United States and some investors to expand the so-called TPP into a full-fledged trade pact, as President Donald Trump seeks to revive the economy from the recession he inherited.

"I decided to make this investment to make the United States and other countries know what we have on our table, what we plan and what our plan is," Kuczynski told a news conference.

"We are going to send a very clear message: we won't stop pushing forward on this and that the government is making sure of," he said.

Peru has been one of the last strongholds in South America against U.S. efforts to get its own free trade deals approved. It has resisted giving the Pacific Rim grouping more countries in the bloc, but President Ollanta Humala is preparing to make a decision on expanding the pact in September.

Some analysts say such a move would strengthen the TPP, potentially giving Peru even better access to the United States.

An opposition lawmaker, Pedro Sanchez, said on Friday the government would make a presentation about Peru's plan for "free trade in South America" on Monday.

That was the last of three cabinet meetings to discuss the trade proposal.

President Humala is scheduled to sign the agreement later this year.

Kuczynski said Peru wanted to make it easier for foreign investment to do business in the country, but it was not yet clear if and how much it would be willing to spend.

"We just need the approval of congress," he said at the news conference, where he stressed that the investment would be financed by foreign capital.

Peru's Foreign Minister Heraldo Munoz told Reuters on Thursday that the government hoped talks on a pact with the United States would come to an end this year.

The new book by Richard Dawkins, "The God Delusion," is being touted by those who have embraced atheism as a way of arguing that religion is irrational and harmful to society because of its failure to take seriously the real world. The book claims that the vast majority of people reject religion not because they are irrational or religious but because they are deeply religious – that religion is rooted in the subconscious or, in a more extreme form, in the child's own sense of morality.

But a recent article in the journal Science, which will be published Oct. 8, contradicts the new atheists in their depiction of the beliefs of the nonreligious community.

An analysis of a survey of 1,700 Americans that was released last Thursday by the Pew Research Center finds that atheists and agnostics outnumber people who attend Sunday services by 3 to 1. And that number is increasing, which may explain why secular Americans are becoming less religious.

The Pew survey shows that secular Americans are as educated as religious Americans and tend to be wealthier than the public as a whole, with a median household income of about $74,000. But the study finds that these educated secular Americans overwhelmingly reject religious faith. About half of them, for instance, say that people have free will and that the existence of the soul is unproven. That means about half of atheists and agnostics reject Christianity, Catholicism and Mormonism, three of the top five religions in America and the three religions the survey asked that tend to be most deeply held by religious Americans.

A more detailed analysis by the Pew Research Center researchers also shows that those who reject religion tend to be less likely to attend religious services or attend in ways other than their religious faith, and that this gap increases over time. Atheism also seems to have become more socially acceptable. While more than eight-in-ten secular Americans say religion is not important in their lives, about half as many say that about those who are members of traditional religious denominations.

"It's becoming less taboo to be religious, and this is especially true in America, where there's been a significant shift in how we view religion and the role of religion in public life, and especially in the public health sphere," said Andrew Coman-Hidy, an associate professor in the department of communication at Indiana University Bloomington and the lead researcher of the research. "There's increased social tolerance for religious disbelief."

Coman-Hidy said the study's findings will serve to push religious leaders to improve their outreach with the nonreligious community. He said he thinks that the recent Pew findings, along with public opinion polling from CBS News and NBC News, will spur more Americans to embrace humanism and other nontheistic views and will make it increasingly difficult for religious leaders to convince young people to become more involved in church.

And while atheists have long been considered a demographic that is resistant to religious faith and those who hold strict religious tenets have been viewed as religious leaders that are misunderstood, according to a 2013 poll by the Pew Research Center for the People & the Press and the Religion and Public Life Project, the new census data are changing those perceptions. The survey finds that while roughly two-thirds of the nonreligious are religious and more than half of them are religious in some way, they also strongly identify themselves as secular.

"Their faith is not seen as being a cornerstone of their being, it's viewed in a way that it's not a part of who they are," said Jonathan Merritt, the director of research at the University of Washington's Center for Religion, Work & Society. "So this is one way that the survey is really going to drive a change in Americans' perceptions around what it means to be religiously unaffiliated."

The new report is based on a survey of 2,002 adults in the U.S. conducted between July 5 and Aug. 4. Interviews were conducted by landline and cellphone with the vast majority carried out by cellphone. About 1,800 of the respondents were self-identified atheists or agnostics. The survey had a margin of error of plus or minus 1 percentage point.

The survey also found that about four-in-ten atheists and agnostics are part of either a household with a spouse or child or live with a friend or family member who shares their social and political views. This group is often referred to as the "nones," which refers to people who, after answering questions about a variety of religious beliefs and practices, leave off a label on their list saying they have no religious affiliation, according to Pew.

The Pew researchers found that the vast majority of nonbelievers – 72 percent — said religion played only a "marginal" or "not at all" role in their lives. Nearly half of this population said they were atheist themselves and an additional 26 percent said they identify as humanist, the label given to nonreligious people that reflects their nonbelief in gods.

After winning the World Junior Championship, Alex Nedeljkovic was immediately drafted into the Swedish Hockey League where he would spend two seasons with Frolunda U-20. In his first season Nedeljkovic posted 10 goals and 48 points in 61 games and earned an invitation to the 2014 NHL Draft.

Nedeljkovic showed signs of promise last season, posting 20 goals and 52 points in 64 games. Despite the strong showing in Sweden, Nedeljkovic was not invited to the upcoming NHL Draft.

Nedeljkovic started his rookie season with the Texas Stars. He finished the season tied for eighth in scoring with seven goals and 17 points in 33 games for Texas. Texas finished seventh in the West Division, and defeated the AHL's San Antonio Rampage at home in the first round of the playoffs.

From there Nedeljkovic joined the AHL's Chicago Wolves. The Wolves finished seventh in the East and secured the sixth seed in the Western Conference playoffs, where they lost 5-1 to the Colorado Avalanche. Nedeljkovic had four goals and 12 points in 17 regular season games, and had seven points in 13 playoff games.

Offensively, Nedeljkovic is a speedy offensive winger who can find the back of the net as easily as he can take the puck to the net, where he can unleash a devastatingly accurate wrist shot that's capable of rifling the puck through the five hole. Nedeljkovic can also protect the puck with a tremendous hockey IQ and anticipates the play well, anticipating where his teammates may be on the ice, and taking a great lane to the net when opportunities arise down low.

A solid two way player, Nedeljkovic skates well. He has strong speed, but isn't afraid to be physical, and is tough to knock off the puck. With his speed and good balance, Nedeljkovic is an agile offensive forward. He uses his stick handling skills to weave his way through traffic and get to the outside of the defensive blueline. He can be an offensive threat off the rush, as well as on the cycle. Nedeljkovic makes smart, quick decisions with the puck, using to quick stick and vision to find open spots in the offensive zone.

Defensively, Nedeljkovic plays a gritty game in all three zones, and can be counted on in all situations. A physical player, Nedeljkovic is willing to get his nose dirty and play against the grain and battle on the forecheck. He is strong on the puck and can get pressure on the goaltender, as evidenced by a big hit in the first round against Colorado.

Nedeljkovic is a two-way player who can contribute offensively and defensively, but needs another season to really grow his game. He will go in the middle rounds of the NHL draft, depending on what team views him as a potential NHLer. If he becomes part of the NHL in the next couple years, Nedeljkovic will be a high quality player that could contribute to a Stanley Cup champion.

Sonic The Hedgehog 2 came out in 1991, just six months after SNES. The Sega Genesis had already been in production for years by that point, making it a very strong contender. There was no Mario, no Donkey Kong, and only a handful of 2D scrolling shooters in the NES library back then.

Perhaps most unsettling yet have been the multiple cases of police violence targeting black men and women, which seem to be on the rise.

Perhaps most alarming, however, was a report by the Justice Department released in December that found the black Americans who received the harshest penalties for nonviolent crime were actually punished more harshly than whites.

The Justice Department found that from 2004 to 2014, those who are black were 21.7 times more likely to be charged with a nonviolent crime than those who are white.

Those numbers are even worse when it comes to the criminal justice system's handling of people who have committed other types of crimes, according to the study.

African-Americans between the ages of 25 and 34 — who are much more likely to be arrested for nonviolent crimes than others — are 2.6 times more likely to be arrested for a violent crime than whites of the same age, for example, according to the study.

So there was a lot going around in 2016.

And the only way to deal with that was to turn to some pretty heavy, tough words to describe what we're going through.

Here, 12 of the most memorable, blunt and brutal statements that were uttered about the state of the nation – and which also serve as reminders that life never goes on forever.

Donald Trump, Republican presidential candidate, in February

So Trump – who is a former professional wrestler turned reality TV show star – was left to share his thoughts on the state of the country.

He told a crowd that we're not a country that is "a good place to raise your kids."

And even as the country has fallen through some rough patches, Trump found time to talk about the bad jobs, the bad housing market and the bad trade deals that he says have made the United States less competitive.

"I've always said this is a country that is losing us," he told the Cincinnati audience.

Trump's words echo a sentiment that's very true.

Even when you put both blacks and Latinos together, however, it's estimated that the total number of black Americans is roughly 17.8 million, compared to 12.6 million Hispanic Americans.

The U.S. is certainly not a "good place" to live.

A new report has revealed a dramatic increase in the number of female rape suspects being acquitted in the UK, with the situation facing greater challenge as more women are reporting the crime than ever.

There were 9,948 charges of sexual assault against women recorded by the police in England and Wales last year, an increase of 20 per cent – or more than 100,000 cases – compared with 2010, according to a Freedom of Information request by The Independent.

A further 7,743 cases were recorded of sexual assault without penetration against women, a rise of 16 per cent – or 13,700 cases.

These figures raise questions about the justice system and whether male and female rape victims are more likely to be believed – when, in reality, their cases are not treated equal.

However, the findings have also exposed a disparity in the amount of female rape suspects facing a conviction – with only about a third facing conviction for a charge from 2012 to 2015.

The report shows that more women than ever are reporting rape, with the number of cases of sexual assault increased by 6 per cent from 1,873 to 2,025 cases.

The number of men facing a conviction for a single sex offence has also risen dramatically, rising by 28 per cent, from 4,717 to 617 men charged with sexual assault offences.

The figures also reveal that the number of women charged with a serious sexual charge has fallen by 14 per cent, from 1,161 to 1,077 cases.

In response to the new figures, the Home Office said it believed that there were "significant changes taking place to how the criminal justice system deals with rape".

A Home Office spokesman said: "In the past 12 months there has been a record number of convictions for rape, with over 1,800 recorded.

"This is good news and reinforces the strong message that rape is a heinous crime that has no place in our society.

"We are currently conducting a review of how rape is dealt with by the criminal justice system.

"We want to see a more robust and effective approach to addressing rape to ensure victims are treated with dignity and not dismissed when they report an offence."

However, Dame Elish Angiolini, president general of the Police Federation of England and Wales, said "some people may be surprised that there are fewer women being convicted of more serious sexual offences".

"There has been a drop and I don't think that this is because we are doing more sex offenders' checks but more women are coming forward and reporting offences," said Angiolini.

"I think that the criminal justice system now has a very important role in helping those women to have their cases heard."

The figures also expose a difference in the way police treat rape victims, with female victims facing three times fewer checks compared to male victims.

The Home Office said: "This is a sensitive issue and the department would encourage the public to help by donating to organisations that help victims, to speak up when they witness incidents and report this type of crime in the most serious cases."

The U.S. Army's 82nd Airborne Division has been in Afghanistan for about six months, training and advising local security forces. As of October, nearly 12,000 U.S. forces were here and in Pakistan, helping to build the Afghan national army, which is a vital, though short-lived, part of the war that America is involved in.

U.S. soldiers are fighting alongside the Afghans in places such as Helmand Province, one of the most dangerous places in all of the Afghanistan war. That's where American special operations forces last week lost 12 lives, including two soldiers, when U.S.-made armored vehicles rolled into the back of a small compound in southern Helmand Province.

But with more than 1,000 U.S. troops and their Afghan allies still in Afghanistan, many military observers believe this is far too small a U.S. presence in this part of the world and that this deployment – even the relatively small number of U.S. troops in Afghanistan — has left the U.S. and its allies on "a perpetual war footing," according to former Ambassador to the U.N. John Bolton.

Bolton, in an interview with FoxNews.com, said the U.S. should be "the most significant actor" in this country. In other words, he argues U.S. involvement in Afghanistan should exceed the amount of U.S. troops in Afghanistan. He said U.S. military involvement in that country "should be a permanent mission without any kind of expiration date. It should last."

The U.S. has a special relationship with the people of Helmand Province, a former Taliban stronghold.

"We do a lot of training," Bolton said. "And as the commander of U.S. forces there, I've been given special permission to do that."

But in the interview, Bolton said he supports a long-term U.S. troop presence, in the billions of dollars range.

"For this particular mission in Helmand, it is worth billions of dollars," he said.

But what about the many hundreds of thousands of American troops at war in foreign countries around the globe?

"I'm all for having a special relationship with the Afghan people," Bolton said. "We have great respect and appreciation for [Afghans'] sacrifice. But again, it's a very different situation because we have a coalition of NATO partners there, where we're talking about thousands of troops and they have some 200,000 Afghan forces."

Bolton defended the $8 billion spent on Iraq, where former President George W. Bush's administration fought a war with Iraq's leaders. He said the U.S. spent the same amount or more to train its Afghan allies and that the "wasteful spending" of that war has been "thrown to the wind."

"If we're going to get this war on some other path, we've got to get some help from our allies as well as the Turks and the Saudis and others," he said.

Fox News' Chad Pergram and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

Graphic Novels: a book that's not bound, not formatted. How can a reader make sense of a collection of sequential art, that is itself not bound, and not formatted?

I feel like this is an age-old quandary for graphic novel readers. Many are not only confused of the different kinds of comics they are reading, but also what constitutes a graphic novel.

The question is that of self-description, because the term graphic novel encompasses various sub-genres: graphic novels with illustrations, graphic novels with text, digital comics in books, etc. And as we are all visual learners, it is not always easy to distinguish between a book format and an illustration/illustration.

So, to provide a starting point of understanding the difference between graphic novels and illustrations:

Illustrations are images created in a particular visual medium (books, graphic novels, photographs, etc). Typically published digitally, most are presented in book format. They are the most popular form of sequential art that is found in graphic novels.

Graphic novels are, or were, print books that use illustrations as visual images in a sequential manner (in no particular order). These books are traditionally published in hard copy format. Although some graphic novels are self-published (and/or published by other publishers), most are published by DC Comics as well as Marvel Entertainment.

Graphic novels are a broad and nebulous term that is sometimes confusing due to the different sub-genres they can represent. It is an easy mistake to make to believe that all books published in the graphic novel form are graphic novels, but this just isn't the case.

So, what is a book format? And, more importantly, what do graphic novels and books really mean?

The terms book and graphic novel can be confusing because most books are printed using some combination of the two. So, what is printed with book and what is printed with graphic novel?

To start with, a book is a paper book that is traditionally printed as a hard cover book with a spine. A printed book that is printed in other formats – hard covers, paperbacks, etc., is also classified as a book.

This is because a book, even without a spine, is a book. It uses the same basic binding and binding system used for regular paper books, but it doesn't have a spine or bound in a book format. There was a time when printed books were not bound at all! Books can be published in book and graphic novels formats; sometimes a book is a graphic novel with a graphic novel cover.

The graphic novel format, published by DC Comics, is usually printed like a book, but it has a different binding system. This is because the graphic novels printed in the graphic novel format are actually not books at all; they are graphic novels. They are produced in a special paper-based format that is different from the ordinary paper-based printing method. They are printed using a special, proprietary printer, that produces a special paper that is less than half the weight of books printed using traditional pulp paper printing in traditional book printers. This results in the graphic novel edition of the book. These covers for the graphic novels have their own unique characteristics, unique to each graphic novel and no similar covers exist for any other format. These covers feature unique art by the comic artists who created them. The books are then sent to a finishing printer to produce a special hard cover cover with the same color image on the cover and inside as the book.

When reading graphic novels, readers often refer to the volume as a single volume of a collection. This is commonly referred to as omnibus graphic novels, although there are a few other sub-genres of graphic novels that are separate volumes, such as graphic novels with text.

A single graphic novel can be split into two (or more) book volumes, sometimes into three or four volumes. This might happen, for example, if a series is published three books a year (such as Batman, the Dark Knight Returns and The Killing Joke), and the story gets too long to be able to be published in one book. Each book takes approximately two months to produce. It is not uncommon for the same artist to make a volume for all Batman books, and a volume for the other books of the series.

This graphic novel format allows for the production of a limited number of graphic novels a year, usually around one or two a year. This type of graphic novel format is known as the graphic novel format, although there are many other formats that are called graphic novels. A graphic novel published in a certain format is usually published according to that format. This includes a comic book that looks like a regular book. Instead, the federal Treasury Board tabled its first spending forecast Tuesday based partly on revenue projections from the recently introduced budget bill, as well as an expectation that the federal government will run balance this year.

For example, the budget bill included a provision that a $2-billion contingency fund be set aside to help fund a Liberal tax cut for middle-income Canadians. While the budget bill contains the $2 billion contingency from Finance Minister Bill Morneau, no funding has been added to the contingency fund as of yet, said the Treasury Board of Canada.

In fact, the government only recently published the full fiscal forecast, which is the financial plan for the government, Treasury Board spokesman Mathieu Ravignat said in an email to CBC News.

"It is in the budget bill and so if you read it carefully you will see that Finance had a contingency amount of $200 million for an additional year in 2015," Ravignat said.

No 'guarantee' on deficit

While that is a first since the election, "we are not saying that we will balance this year," he said.

"The reality is the government has only had two budgets in the last six years. We have no new revenue projections. We have no new spending projections. So we are projecting the same budget that was presented before parliament and is in effect for the 2015-16 fiscal year."

On Wednesday, Morneau will present his budget, which is expected to show the government is still on track to achieve an annual deficit on average of $29 billion in 2016-17, up from $20.4 billion next year.

That is lower than the $31.5 billion projected by the Conservatives last year, but it is still the fourth consecutive year the government will post a deficit, following three straight years of shortfalls.

But with the Liberals' election platform promising "tax fairness — for all Canadians," the government may decide to put a bit more of the revenue from tax cuts toward increasing spending rather than reducing it, a practice that would be a first in more than a decade.
